title: Behavior
description: What an actor can do, named in domain terms. A behaviour is the unit a person asks for and the unit a test is written against: 'sign in', not 'fill_login_email'. How the UI happens to do it belongs in realization[] and nowhere else, because a behaviour named after its first DOM step is not a behaviour - it is a step wearing a behaviour's name, and it forces every consumer to reassemble the user's intent from the implementation.

name.description: Verb phrase in the application's own language: login, add_to_cart, reset_password, list_projects. Must not name a mechanism - fill_login_email is refused, because it names the page rather than the outcome.

kind.description: Coarse classification. 'composite' means the behaviour is defined only by composed_of; a composite whose parts are not all realized is a claim about the application the model cannot support.

actor.description: Role that can perform this behaviour, when it is actor-specific. Must equal an application.actors[].id.

output.description: What the behaviour yields, named semantically: session, project, order. A behaviour whose output is read by a later behaviour is a dependency the walk can be checked against.

contract.description: What performing this behaviour MEANS, separately from how one walk performed it. `realization[]` is an observation; this is the claim that observation is evidence about, and the two are deliberately separate documents of different kinds: a UI change invalidates the realization and leaves the behaviour intact, and a test written against the contract still asserts the same thing after the markup is rewritten.

assertions.description: Checks that hold once the behaviour has been performed, independent of which surface it started from.

realization.description: The ordered steps that perform this behaviour. A behaviour is realized by steps, never composed of them: steps are how, composed_of is what. A behaviour with a non-empty realization and a non-empty composed_of has two answers to one question.

composed_of.description: Other behaviours this one is made of, in order. Names behaviours, never steps, and each member must itself be realizable.

behaviorId.description: Behaviours get their own id namespace rather than reusing capabilityId, because the capability pattern (^cap...) would reject behavior_login, and widening it would let a document that has no capabilities keep minting cap_ ids.

actorId.description: Must equal an id in application.actors[]. Kept loose here because the actor vocabulary is owned by the application document, and the join is what matters, not the spelling.

behaviorContract.description: The declared meaning of a behaviour: what has to be true before it, what it establishes, what it can lead to, and what its inputs are. Every entry is a claim about a walk and carries the status of the evidence behind it, so a contract cannot present a plausible outcome as an observed one. A projection derives this from the run's own evidence and adds nothing: an outcome the walk never exercised is absent rather than guessed, and a behaviour whose refusal path was never explored says so by having exactly the outcomes it was seen to produce.

parameters.description: The behaviour's inputs, as bindings a test resolves at run time. `input` from common.schema.json declares the types and is what a step's {{param}} template is checked against; this says which of those inputs carries a value the page declines to read back, which is the difference between test data a generator may write into the file and test data it may only read from the environment.

preconditions.description: What must already be true. The projection fills these with the states the walk actually performed the behaviour from, because that is the only precondition this run can vouch for - a precondition nobody exercised is a claim about a walk that did not happen.

postconditions.description: What is true once the behaviour has been performed. Same shape as preconditions, and it nests none of them: a postcondition is a fact this behaviour is answerable for, which is what a test asserts and a precondition is not.

outcomes.description: Where performing the behaviour can leave the application. `postconditions` says what holds; this says which observed end each holds at, keyed by the state a test can check. The two are not the same claim: a behaviour that can end in a refusal has two outcomes and might share a postcondition with neither.

behaviorParameter.description: One input of the behaviour, as a binding. The value is never here: a parameter is a name a test resolves, and a contract that stored the credential it was performed with would be the credential in the durable artefact, which is the thing the mask exists to prevent.

name.description: Must equal a key of `input`, which is where the declared type lives.

sensitive.description: True when a step of the realization supplied a value into a field the page declines to read back. It is the recorder's own test rather than a guess about a name: the reading says the field withheld its value, and the step says which input fed it. A sensitive parameter must be resolved from the environment, never written into generated test data.

behaviorOutcome.description: One way the behaviour can end. `status` is what keeps the contract honest: 'observed' means the walk reached this state by performing the behaviour, and anything weaker must say so, because a plausible failure path carried as a fact is worse than an absent one - it is a test that passes for the wrong reason.

to_state.description: The state the application is left in. Must resolve to a declared state, which is what makes an outcome checkable rather than a sentence.

status.description: The D9/D11 level of this outcome: observed when a reading saw the application arrive there, inferred when the projection derived it from an edge, modelled when a person declared it. The three are ordinary levels of a claim, and this field is the one place a contract can get one wrong.

behaviorStep.description: One interaction, as the application actually performed it. This is the mechanism layer: a step may be renamed, reordered or dropped without changing what the actor asked for, which is why nothing outside realization[] is allowed to depend on a step's identity.

element.description: Element acted on. Must resolve to an element declared by the state the walk was in when the step ran - derived from that state's declaration, never taken on trust from the model.

value.description: Literal value, or a {{param}} template bound to a declared input or a journey step's arguments. A concrete value is only acceptable when it was observed; a redacted field is recorded honestly as [set] rather than guessed.

purpose.description: Why this step is in the behaviour, in the behaviour's own terms: enter_credentials, submit, dismiss_banner. This is what makes a step reviewable on its own, and what survives when the step's element is renamed.

arguments.description: Concrete values observed for this step, when they differ from value. Recorded as observed, redacted as [set].

effects.description: What this step changed. Step-scoped effects exist because a multi-step behaviour can land its state only on the last step, and without them the only way to say which step did the work is to re-read the observations.
